name: Cho gio (cạo gió)

card.summary: Vietnamese form of gua sha, a skin-scraping practice that now overlaps with facial gua sha used for a more sculpted, refreshed look.
card.note: Produces petechiae that resemble bruises; skin trauma is common.

quick.overview:
Cạo gió ("scraping wind") is the Vietnamese term for gua sha, a traditional East and Southeast Asian practice of scraping oiled skin with a smooth tool such as a coin or spoon until reddish marks appear.

Traditionally it is a home remedy; its appearance link comes from the facial gua sha trend, where lighter strokes are used for skin refresh and facial contouring.
quick.how: Traditional cạo gió uses firm, one-direction strokes with a blunt tool over oiled skin until marks appear. Facial gua sha uses lighter pressure with a stone tool.
quick.risks: Treatment nearly always causes some skin trauma such as redness and bruising; burns, infection with unsterilised tools and rare serious injury are reported. The marks have been misread as signs of abuse.

lead: Cạo gió is the Vietnamese name for gua sha, a practice in which a smooth object scrapes the skin along muscles to produce petechiae, the red or purple marks called sha.[1]

For looks, the connection is facial gua sha, which uses lighter pressure and was promoted by beauty influencers on TikTok in 2021-2022 for lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation.[1] The wiki entry exists because the Vietnamese variant is often cited as the origin of the technique.
A pilot study in healthy subjects examined gua sha's effect on microcirculation of surface tissue.[2]

chain: Claimed refreshed, more defined face (facial version)
angle.text: Facial gua sha is used for a refreshed, contoured look; benefits are claimed by practitioners and beauty influencers.

paras: Gua means to scrape and sha refers to the marks left behind; in traditional Chinese medicine practitioners link them with qi and blood stagnation. Vietnamese communities practise cạo gió as a home remedy.[1]
A 2007 pilot study in healthy subjects measured gua sha's effects on surface-tissue microcirculation.[2] Wikipedia states that gua sha lacks high-quality evidence of clinical benefit.[1]

Nearly every treatment causes some skin trauma; burns, hematuria, and infection from unsterilised tools have been reported, and rare serious harms such as brain bleeding. The marks can be mistaken for abuse.[1]
